recordings.text: Fun fact! With a jellyfish gene, cats, mice, and even bacteria can glow green under blue light. How? The genetic code is nearly universal, so their cells can build the same glowing protein! That’s gene expression! DNA is copied into RNA, then ribosomes read the message to build a protein. Swipe to explore, and tap me for a hand. Let’s find the gene!
recordings.title: Opening · Listen

recordings.text: Message delivered! You practiced transcription, processing, translation, folding, and protein finishing. You can start a new round with a different stop codon, or tap Done to return to the lesson.
recordings.title: Message delivered!

recordings.text:
Let’s put the whole journey together.

Protein synthesis is a core mechanism of gene expression: DNA → RNA → Protein. Transcription copies a specific gene’s DNA sequence into complementary RNA. Translation decodes mRNA to assemble amino acids into a polypeptide. Folding and processing help produce a functional protein.
recordings.title: The big picture

recordings.text:
First, let’s find the start of a gene.

Transcription occurs in the nucleus of eukaryotes; in the cytoplasm of prokaryotes. In eukaryotes, transcription factors bind promoters or distant enhancers, helping attract RNA polymerase. TATA-binding protein is one example of a transcription factor. RNA polymerase attaches at the promoter and unzips DNA, exposing the template strand.
recordings.title: Find the gene

recordings.text:
Now the cell writes an RNA copy of the gene.

RNA polymerase reads the DNA template 3′ → 5′. It adds complementary RNA nucleotides only to the growing 3′ end, so RNA is built 5′ → 3′. DNA → RNA pairing: A → U (uracil), T → A, G → C, C → G.
recordings.title: Write the RNA

recordings.text:
The RNA message is ready to be released.

RNA polymerase reaches a DNA terminator sequence. The enzyme detaches and releases the completed RNA transcript. The DNA rewinds into its double helix.
recordings.title: Release the message

recordings.text:
Before this message leaves the nucleus, it gets a little editing.

Before pre-mRNA leaves the nucleus, a modified-nucleotide 5′ cap protects it from cytoplasmic degradation and helps ribosome binding. A poly A tail adds 100–200 adenine nucleotides at the 3′ end, improving stability and translation efficiency. Splicing: small catalytic RNAs and proteins remove non-coding introns and join retained exons. The resulting mature mRNA exits the nucleus and carries its genetic recipe to the cytoplasm.
recordings.title: Edit the message

recordings.text:
Next, the message meets the ribosome.

Translation occurs at ribosomes in the cytoplasm: free or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. In the eukaryotic sequence shown, the small ribosomal subunit binds the mRNA’s 5′ cap. An initiator tRNA brings methionine (Met). Its anticodon UAC pairs with the start codon AUG. The large ribosomal subunit joins to complete the ribosome.
recordings.title: Meet the ribosome

recordings.text:
Now the ribosome links amino acids into a growing chain.

A second tRNA matches the adjacent mRNA codon, delivering its specific amino acid. The ribosome forms a covalent peptide bond between amino acids and moves one codon along mRNA, 5′ → 3′. The first, now empty tRNA leaves to pick up another amino acid in the cytosol. Elongation factors help repeat delivery and movement, lengthening the polypeptide one codon at a time.
recordings.title: Link the amino acids

recordings.text:
A stop signal tells the ribosome when the chain is finished.

The ribosome reaches a stop codon: UGA, UAA, or UAG. No tRNA corresponds to a stop codon. A release factor protein binds instead. The polypeptide is released; the ribosomal subunits, tRNA, and mRNA separate.
recordings.title: Stop and release

recordings.text:
The new chain needs to fold into a useful shape.

The polypeptide folds into its functional 3D shape. Chaperone proteins help and stabilize the folding process.
recordings.title: Find the final shape

recordings.text:
Some proteins need a few finishing touches.

Cleavage: enzymes cut some proteins into smaller functional pieces. Example: proinsulin → insulin, a 51-amino-acid product. Assembly: some proteins combine several polypeptide chains. Hemoglobin has four subunits.
recordings.title: The finishing touches

recordings.text: Genome, chromosome & gene. Genome: all the genetic material within a cell. Chromosome: a discrete package of DNA wrapped around specialized histone proteins in the nucleus. Gene: a DNA segment encoding a specific protein or functional RNA.
recordings.title: Genome, chromosome & gene

recordings.text: The template strand. The template strand is the DNA strand actually transcribed into RNA. RNA polymerase reads it 3′ → 5′ and builds RNA 5′ → 3′, adding to the 3′ end. Pairing: DNA A → RNA U, T → A, G → C, C → G. U means uracil.
recordings.title: The template strand

recordings.text: RNA polymerase. Attaches to DNA at a promoter, unzips the double helix, and builds complementary RNA. At termination, it detaches and releases the RNA transcript; the DNA rewinds.
recordings.title: RNA polymerase

recordings.text: Promoter & terminator. Promoter: a DNA sequence marking where transcription begins. Terminator: a DNA sequence signaling the end of transcription.
recordings.title: Promoter & terminator

recordings.text: Transcription factors. In eukaryotes, transcription factors bind promoters or distant enhancers, attracting RNA polymerase. TATA-binding protein is one example of a transcription factor.
recordings.title: Transcription factors

recordings.text: mRNA & codons. Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries the genetic recipe from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. A codon is three consecutive mRNA bases specifying one amino acid or a stop signal. The genetic code matches 64 triplet codons to 20 amino acids or stop signals.
recordings.title: mRNA & codons

recordings.text: tRNA & anticodon. Transfer RNA (tRNA) carries a specific amino acid at one end and a three-base anticodon loop at the other. The anticodon binds its complementary mRNA codon. At initiation, 5′-AUG-3′ pairs with 3′-UAC-5′. The initiator tRNA carries methionine (Met). Empty tRNA leaves to pick up another amino acid in the cytosol.
recordings.title: tRNA & anticodon

recordings.text: rRNA & ribosome. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and proteins form the ribosome’s small and large subunits. Ribosomes are the site of translation, free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The small subunit binds first; the large subunit joins after the initiator tRNA matches AUG.
recordings.title: rRNA & ribosome

recordings.text: The mRNA editing crew. The 5′ cap is a modified nucleotide: protection from degradation and help with ribosome binding. The 3′ poly A tail adds 100–200 adenines for stability and translation efficiency. Small catalytic RNAs and proteins remove non-coding introns and join retained exons. Mature mRNA then leaves the nucleus.
recordings.title: The mRNA editing crew

recordings.text: Peptide bonds & elongation factors. The ribosome makes covalent peptide bonds between amino acids. Elongation factors help tRNAs deliver amino acids as the ribosome advances 5′ → 3′, one codon at a time. The growing amino acid chain is a polypeptide.
recordings.title: Peptide bonds & elongation factors

recordings.text: Stop codons & release factors. The three stop codons are UGA, UAA, and UAG. Stop codons have no matching tRNA. Release factor proteins bind instead. Release factors trigger polypeptide release and separation of ribosomal subunits, tRNA, and mRNA.
recordings.title: Stop codons & release factors

recordings.text: Chaperone proteins. A polypeptide folds into its functional 3D protein shape. Chaperone proteins aid and stabilize folding.
recordings.title: Chaperone proteins

recordings.text: Cleavage & assembly. Cleavage enzymes cut some proteins into functional pieces: proinsulin → 51-amino-acid insulin. Assembly brings separate polypeptide chains together: hemoglobin has four subunits.
recordings.title: Cleavage & assembly
